title: There May Not Be an iPhone 18 This Year
gist: Apple is expected to launch only its premium iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and a first foldable device at its September 9 event, delaying the base iPhone 18 to spring 2027 — a 'premiumization' strategy analysts tie to an industry-wide memory shortage that is pushing up component costs and smartphone prices broadly.

insights.claim: Based on leaks and analyst expectations, Apple is expected to announce only the premium iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and a first Apple foldable device at its September 9 event, holding off on the base iPhone 18 until spring 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A shift away from launching a full iPhone lineup simultaneously would change Apple's revenue timing and could pressure unit volumes of its historically strongest quarter differently than in past years.
insights.locator: Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill

insights.claim: IDC senior director Nabila Popal says spreading iPhone launches across two seasons is a smart strategic move because it lets Apple balance revenue between its typically strong fourth quarter and its usually weaker following spring quarter.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Reframes the delayed base-model launch as a deliberate revenue-smoothing tactic rather than a supply-constraint accident, which matters for how analysts should model Apple's quarterly seasonality going forward.
insights.quote: Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.
insights.locator: Popal says it's a smart strategic move

insights.claim: Nabila Popal describes Apple's strategy as a 'premiumization' of devices, in which the company leans into higher prices for its Pro and Pro Max lineup rather than absorbing rising costs on a cheaper base model.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Suggests Apple's near-term profit strategy is shifting mix toward higher-margin premium devices, a trend investors would want reflected in average-selling-price and margin expectations.
insights.locator: It's part of a 'premiumization' of devices

themes.theme: Memory shortage driving industry-wide price increases

insights.claim: An ongoing memory shortage has raised component and manufacturing costs across the smartphone industry, and former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged in June that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with those costs.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific macro supply-chain shock (memory shortage) as the root cause behind Apple's product-strategy and pricing changes, a factor likely to affect other device makers as well.
insights.locator: It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage

insights.claim: When component costs rise, companies generally have three options — absorb the costs, raise prices, or delay cheaper models — and Apple appears to be choosing to delay its cheaper iPhone models rather than raise their prices or eat the cost increase.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Gives investors a simple mental model for interpreting how hardware makers respond to component-cost shocks, useful for anticipating peers' pricing decisions in the same memory-shortage environment.

insights.claim: Rising component costs are making less-expensive phones less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, with leading smartphone brands increasingly viewing budget models as far less economical to produce.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Signals a broader industry pullback from budget smartphone segments, which could shift competitive dynamics and pricing power toward premium-focused manufacturers.
insights.locator: Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases

insights.claim: Global Electronics Association chief economist Shawn DuBravac says he expects the historical pattern of technology's deflationary pressure to eventually flow through to consumers again, even though it will take time for markets to solidify.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Offers a longer-run counterpoint to near-term price hikes, suggesting current elevated smartphone prices from the memory shortage may not be permanent.
insights.quote: Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer
insights.locator: Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association

themes.theme: Foldables, financing, and the used-phone market

insights.claim: Foldable phones are seeing higher prices than ever, with Samsung's entire 2026 Galaxy Z fold lineup, Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Motorola's 2026 Razr models all increasing in price, while Apple's rumored first foldable iPhone is expected to cost around $2,000.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Establishes a competitive price ceiling across the foldable category, positioning Apple's expected $2,000 price point within a broader industry trend of rising foldable prices rather than an outlier.
insights.locator: That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones

insights.claim: Apple launched an iPhone leasing program in July that lets customers pay a monthly fee to use the newest iPhones and swap them for new devices as they release, a move ownership advocates have criticized for keeping buyers from truly owning their device.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Shows Apple actively converting hardware sales into recurring subscription-like revenue, a business-model shift relevant to how investors value Apple's device segment going forward.
insights.locator: In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program

insights.claim: IDC's Nabila Popal says most consumers already buy Apple phones through financing or trade-in programs, and expects Apple to lean into more aggressive trade-in offers to cushion the impact of rising prices.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Indicates that financing/trade-in mechanics, not sticker price alone, are now the primary lever Apple uses to sustain unit demand as list prices climb.
insights.quote: The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs
insights.locator: The way most consumers buy Apple phones

insights.claim: Demand for refurbished smartphones has been climbing, with used-device sales growing even as new phone sales slow, as more consumers look to save money or buy more eco-friendly products.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Points to a growing secondary/refurbished market as a demand-side response to rising new-device prices, a trend that could weigh on new iPhone unit growth.
insights.locator: On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices

insights.claim: Nabila Popal summarizes the current market shift bluntly, saying the era of the cheap smartphone is over.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A blunt, quotable framing of the article's core takeaway: rising component costs are structurally raising smartphone price floors industry-wide, not just at Apple.
insights.quote: The days of the cheap smartphone are over
insights.locator: 'The days of the cheap smartphone are over.'
